title: Mobilizing Stem Cells and Photopheresis: G-CSF, Plerixafor, ECP
summary: How G-CSF and the CXCR4 antagonist plerixafor mobilize CD34+ cells for apheresis, how grafts are dosed, and how extracorporeal photopheresis treats and returns a patient’s white cells.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 42 Hits 4, 8, 9 and 14. Checked against Hequet 2015, De Clercq 2019, Bonig 2015, Arora & Setia 2017 and Knobler 2014. Hit 8 limits plerixafor to NHL/myeloma patients “failing G-CSF”; De Clercq 2019 describes approval for autologous mobilization in NHL and myeloma (with G-CSF) (register flag rv-plerixafor-label). Hit 4 uses 2.5 × 10⁶ CD34+/kg; Hequet 2015 gives ≥ 2 × 10⁶/kg per graft (see the Ch. 43 needs-verification entry). Not taught: G-CSF split into two doses and the 16 µg/kg ceiling, bone pain in ~80%, chronic GVHD above 8 × 10⁶/kg, MNC/CFU-GM doses, product hematocrit < 7%, 24-hour sun avoidance (Arora: 48 h) and ASFA categories for ECP.

objectives: Explain how G-CSF and plerixafor mobilize CD34+ cells and how grafts are dosed.
Distinguish mobilization of healthy donors from mobilization of patients with lymphoma or myeloma.
Describe the extracorporeal photopheresis process, aftercare and main indications.

scenes.title: Not enough CD34+ cells
scenes.altText: Two cards. Card A: a man with multiple myeloma, day 5 of G-CSF; peripheral blood CD34+ count low; first apheresis collects 0.9 × 10⁶ CD34+/kg. Card B: a healthy sibling donor for an allogeneic transplant, starting G-CSF tomorrow. A third card: a patient with erythrodermic cutaneous T-cell lymphoma booked for “photopheresis.” A question token: “What moves stem cells into blood — and what is photopheresis?” The cartoon scientist looks at a CD34 counter.

cues.text: A man with myeloma is on day five of G-CSF. His first apheresis yields only 0.9 million CD34-positive cells per kilogram.
His healthy sister will donate stem cells for someone else and starts G-CSF tomorrow.
And down the hall, a patient with erythrodermic cutaneous T-cell lymphoma is booked for photopheresis. Two apheresis services, two very different products.

scenes.title: Stem cells are anchored in marrow
scenes.altText: A marrow niche (schematic): an HPC holds onto a stromal cell through the receptor CXCR4 binding its ligand SDF-1 (CXCL12). G-CSF arrow: stimulates myelopoiesis and loosens the anchoring, so CD34+ cells spill into blood. A target card: at least 2 × 10⁶ CD34+ cells/kg per graft (one review; centres differ); myeloma programmes often aim for 4 × 10⁶/kg per graft to allow two transplants. A note: CD34+ cells are counted by flow cytometry.

cues.text: Hematopoietic progenitor cells live anchored in the marrow. One key tether is the receptor CXCR4 on the stem cell, holding on to its ligand, SDF-1, also called CXCL12.
G-CSF stimulates white-cell production and loosens the anchoring, so CD34-positive cells spill into the blood, where apheresis can collect them.
The product is measured in CD34-positive cells per kilogram of the recipient’s body weight, counted by flow cytometry.
One review gives a minimum of 2 million CD34-positive cells per kilogram per graft, with centres differing.
Myeloma programmes often aim for 4 million per kilogram per graft, so there is enough for two transplants.

props.label: G-CSF: loosens the anchor → CD34+ into blood

scenes.title: G-CSF for donors, plerixafor for poor mobilizers
scenes.altText: Two lanes. Healthy donor lane: G-CSF (filgrastim or lenograstim) 10 µg/kg/day for 4–5 days before apheresis; adverse effects include bone pain (more with higher doses), flu-like symptoms, headache, and rarely splenic rupture. Patient lane: plerixafor — a reversible CXCR4 antagonist that blocks the CXCR4/SDF-1 tether; best used together with G-CSF; FDA-approved in 2008 for autologous mobilization in non-Hodgkin lymphoma and multiple myeloma; adding it to G-CSF sharply cut mobilization failure in trials. A note: one 2015 review states plerixafor is not approved for healthy donors in the US or most countries.

cues.text: Healthy donors usually receive G-CSF, filgrastim or lenograstim, about 10 micrograms per kilogram per day for four to five days before collection.
Expect bone pain, more so at higher doses, plus flu-like symptoms and headache. Splenic rupture is rare but recognised.
For patients who mobilize poorly, plerixafor cuts the tether. It reversibly blocks CXCR4, so stem cells let go of SDF-1 and enter the blood.
It works best combined with G-CSF. The FDA approved it in 2008 for autologous mobilization in non-Hodgkin lymphoma and multiple myeloma.
It is not approved for healthy donors in the US or most countries. So patient A, the myeloma patient, is the plerixafor candidate; his sister gets G-CSF.

props.label: Not approved for healthy donors (US, most countries)

scenes.title: Photopheresis: treat the white cells, return them
scenes.altText: An ECP circuit (schematic): blood is drawn, a leukocyte-rich (buffy coat) fraction is separated, 8-methoxypsoralen (8-MOP) is added, the fraction is exposed to UVA light, and the treated cells are reinfused. Early methods gave oral 8-MOP (nausea, eye effects); modern systems add it to the collected fraction. Photoactivation time is calculated from the fraction’s volume and hematocrit — red cells get in the way of the light. Aftercare card: high-SPF sunscreen and UVA-protective sunglasses after each session (one review: 48 hours). Indications card: cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, with higher response rates in erythrodermic disease; also graft-versus-host disease. Back to the hook: C’s product is treated white cells returned to the same patient.

cues.text: Extracorporeal photopheresis collects a white-cell-rich buffy-coat fraction, treats it, and gives it back to the same patient.
The fraction is mixed with 8-methoxypsoralen and exposed to ultraviolet A light. Early methods gave the drug by mouth; modern systems add it to the collected cells.
The machine calculates light exposure from the fraction’s volume and hematocrit, because red cells get in the way of the light.
After each session, patients use high-SPF sunscreen and UVA sunglasses. One review advises 48 hours.
The classic indication is cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, with better responses in erythrodermic disease, and it is also used in graft-versus-host disease.

props.label: Light dose set by volume + hematocrit

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “Give plerixafor to the healthy sibling donor” (✓ approved for autologous NHL/myeloma mobilization; not for healthy donors in the US); “Plerixafor is only for patients who already failed G-CSF” (✓ the label pairs it with G-CSF in NHL and myeloma); “Photopheresis destroys the collected cells and discards them” (✓ the treated cells are returned to the patient).

cues.text: Trap one: give plerixafor to the healthy sibling. It is approved for autologous mobilization in lymphoma and myeloma, not for healthy donors in the US.
Trap two: plerixafor is only for patients who already failed G-CSF. Its approval pairs it with G-CSF in lymphoma and myeloma; failure rescue is one use, not the definition.
Trap three: photopheresis discards the collected cells. The treated cells are returned to the patient.

props.title: ✗ “Plerixafor only after G-CSF failure.”
lines: ✓ Label: with G-CSF in NHL and myeloma

scenes.title: Loosen the anchor, cut the tether, light the buffy coat
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “G-CSF loosens the anchor; plerixafor cuts the CXCR4 tether; ECP lights the buffy coat and sends it home.” Three tokens. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: G-CSF loosens the anchor, plerixafor cuts the CXCR4 tether, and photopheresis lights up the buffy coat and sends it home.
Where it breaks: G-CSF acts in more ways than one anchor; CD34 targets differ between centres and diseases; and ECP’s immune effects are not fully understood.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Donors: G-CSF 10 µg/kg/day × 4–5 days · patients: plerixafor (CXCR4) + G-CSF for NHL/myeloma · ≥ ~2 × 10⁶ CD34+/kg per graft”, “ECP: buffy coat + 8-MOP + UVA → reinfused · sun protection · CTCL, GVHD”.

cues.text: Healthy donors mobilize with G-CSF, patients with lymphoma or myeloma can add plerixafor, grafts are dosed in CD34-positive cells per kilogram, and photopheresis returns light-treated white cells.

props.label: Donor: G-CSF 10 µg/kg/d × 4–5 d · patient: plerixafor + G-CSF · ≥ ~2 × 10⁶ CD34+/kg
ECP: buffy coat + 8-MOP + UVA → reinfused · sun protection · CTCL, GVHD

explanation.what: Plain language: stem cells are normally held in the marrow; drugs can release them into blood for collection. Photopheresis collects a patient’s white cells, treats them with a light-activated drug and gives them back. Scientific terms: hematopoietic progenitor cells (HPC), CD34+, G-CSF (filgrastim, lenograstim), CXCR4, SDF-1 (CXCL12), plerixafor (AMD3100), extracorporeal photopheresis (ECP), 8-methoxypsoralen (8-MOP), UVA.
explanation.why: CXCR4 on HPCs binds stromal SDF-1, tethering them in marrow. Plerixafor reversibly antagonizes CXCR4; G-CSF mobilizes CD34+ cells through broader marrow effects. In ECP, 8-MOP activated by UVA alters the treated leukocytes; red cells in the fraction impede light delivery.
explanation.measure: CD34+ cells by flow cytometry per kg recipient weight; minimum ~2 × 10⁶/kg per graft (Hequet 2015; centres differ); myeloma often 4 × 10⁶/kg per graft. Healthy donors: G-CSF 10 µg/kg/day for 4–5 days before apheresis. Plerixafor: FDA 2008 for autologous mobilization in NHL and multiple myeloma with G-CSF; standard dose 240 µg/kg. ECP light exposure calculated from fraction volume and hematocrit.
explanation.differs: Healthy allogeneic donors (G-CSF; plerixafor not approved in the US) vs autologous patients (G-CSF ± plerixafor, chemotherapy-based strategies). ECP (cells treated and returned) vs therapeutic plasma exchange (plasma removed and replaced).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: plerixafor mechanism and indication, G-CSF side effects, CD34+ dose per kg, and the ECP sequence (buffy coat, 8-MOP, UVA, reinfusion) with CTCL as the classic indication.

comparisons.title: Photopheresis vs plasma exchange
comparisons.distinguisher: What is collected and whether it is returned.

mnemonic.text: G-CSF loosens the anchor; plerixafor cuts the CXCR4 tether; ECP lights the buffy coat and sends it home.
mnemonic.explanation: G-CSF mobilizes CD34+ cells; plerixafor blocks CXCR4/SDF-1; ECP treats white cells with 8-MOP and UVA and reinfuses them.
mnemonic.limitation: G-CSF works through several mechanisms; CD34+ targets differ between centres and diseases; ECP’s immune effects are not fully understood.

questions.stem: How does plerixafor mobilize hematopoietic progenitor cells?

options.text: It reversibly blocks CXCR4, releasing cells from SDF-1 (CXCL12) on marrow stroma
options.rationale: Correct. Plerixafor is a CXCR4 antagonist that interrupts the CXCR4/SDF-1 tether.
Incorrect. That is G-CSF’s action; plerixafor is usually given with G-CSF.
Incorrect. It blocks a receptor interaction; it is not cytotoxic.

options.text: It increases CD34 expression on mature neutrophils
options.rationale: Incorrect. CD34 marks progenitor cells, not mature neutrophils.

questions.stem: A healthy sibling will donate peripheral blood stem cells. Which mobilization regimen is standard?

options.text: G-CSF about 10 µg/kg/day for 4–5 days before apheresis
options.rationale: Correct. This is the usual healthy-donor regimen; expect bone pain and flu-like symptoms.
Incorrect. Plerixafor is approved for autologous mobilization in NHL and myeloma, not for healthy donors in the US.
Incorrect. Chemotherapy-based mobilization is a patient strategy, not used in healthy donors.
Incorrect. Without mobilization, circulating CD34+ counts are too low for an adequate harvest.

options.text: Collect a buffy-coat fraction, add 8-methoxypsoralen, expose to UVA, reinfuse to the patient
options.rationale: Correct. ECP treats the patient’s leukocytes and returns them.

options.text: Remove plasma and replace it with albumin
options.rationale: Incorrect. That describes therapeutic plasma exchange.

options.text: Irradiate donor red cells with gamma rays before transfusion
options.rationale: Incorrect. That describes component irradiation to prevent TA-GVHD.

options.text: Collect CD34+ cells and freeze them for transplant

claims.text: CXCR4/SDF-1 tether; G-CSF mobilization; healthy donors 10 µg/kg/day for 4–5 days; bone pain dose-related; rare splenic rupture.
Plerixafor reversible CXCR4 antagonist, with G-CSF; FDA 2008 autologous NHL/MM; not approved for healthy donors in US/most countries.
Minimum ~2 × 10⁶ CD34+/kg per graft; MM often 4 × 10⁶/kg per graft.
ECP: leukocyte fraction + 8-MOP + UVA, reinfused; light dose from volume and hematocrit; sun protection (48 h in one review); CTCL (erythrodermic) and GVHD.
G-CSF split doses and > 16 µg/kg no gain; bone pain ~80%; chronic GVHD above 8 × 10⁶/kg; product Hct < 7%; 24 h sun avoidance; ASFA I/1B for erythrodermic CTCL.
